How we built our multi-agent research system

components.name: O modelo como componente
components.desc: Escolha de modelo, tokens, não determinismo, tool calling, saída estruturada, prompt caching.

components.name: Engenharia de contexto
components.desc: O que o modelo vê: RAG, memória, sumarização e compactação, grafos de conhecimento.

components.name: Ferramentas e MCP
components.desc: Interface agente-computador: descrição de ferramentas, MCP, function calling, uso de navegador.

components.name: Controle de fluxo
components.desc: Workflow ou agente, ReAct, roteamento, planejamento, reflexão, condição de parada, harness.

components.name: Multi-agente
components.desc: Orquestrador e trabalhadores, subagentes, handoff, comunicação entre agentes.

components.name: Humano e interface
components.desc: UX de agente, streaming, aprovação, human-in-the-loop, interface gerada, tools de front-end.

components.name: Segurança e guardrails
components.desc: Prompt injection, permissões, sandbox, identidade do agente, proteção de dados.

components.name: Custo, latência e confiabilidade
components.desc: Servir em escala, roteamento de modelo por custo, cache, retry, SLA.

components.name: Estado e execução durável
components.desc: Checkpoints, agentes longos e em segundo plano, retomada, memória entre sessões.

components.name: Avaliação
components.desc: Evals offline, LLM como juiz, rubricas, benchmarks, avaliação online.

components.name: Observabilidade
components.desc: Traces e monitoramento de agentes e aplicações com LLM.

components.name: Loops de melhoria
components.desc: Data flywheel, agentes que se melhoram, RL com dado de produção, loops de verificação.

components.name: Software factory
components.desc: Agentes de código organizados em linha de produção: do ticket ao código em produção, com portões de verificação. Palestras com o conceito no título têm adequação máxima.

components.name: Ontologias
components.desc: Ontologias, grafos de conhecimento, camada semântica, GraphRAG e modelagem de domínio para agentes.

videos.t: How Google DeepMind is researching the next Frontier of AI for Gemini — Raia Hadsell, VP of Research
ch: Introduction

Advanced Embedding Models: Raia discusses the importance of embedding models for fast retrieval and recognition, similar to how the human brain uses 'Jennifer Aniston cells' to identify concepts across modalities. She highlights Gemini Embeddings 2, a fully omnimodal model that processes text, video, and audio into unified semantic vectors.
AI for Weather Forecasting: The team has developed revolutionary models for atmospheric prediction, moving away from traditional physics simulations. Notable breakthroughs include:
GraphCast: A spherical graph neural network that provides accurate 15-day weather forecasts.
GenCast: A probabilistic model that offers higher efficiency and accuracy (97% of the time compared to gold-standard benchmarks).
FGN: A functional generative network that directly predicts cyclone behavior, which is currently being utilized by the US National Hurricane Center.

World Models: Hadsell introduces Genie, a project focused on creating interactive, real-time environments. Starting from Genie 1 (2D platformers) and progressing to Genie 3, these models allow users to create and interact with high-quality, 3D photorealistic worlds. These environments demonstrate capabilities like memory, consistency, and the ability to be dynamically prompted by the user to change the surroundings in real-time.

videos.t: The Friction is Your Judgment — Armin Ronacher & Cristina Poncela Cubeiro, Earendil
ch: The Problem
The Psychological Trap: Because AI tools are addictive and make coding feel effortless, engineers often stop taking the time to design, review, and truly understand the code being generated.

The Engineering Challenge: Agents are optimized for producing code that runs, not code that is maintainable or architecturally sound. This often results in "slop"—code that creates unexpected failure conditions and entropy
Agent-Legible Codebases: To maximize AI effectiveness, the speakers suggest designing codebases as infrastructure. This includes:
Mechanical Enforcement through strict linting (e.g., no bare catch-alls, unique function names, and avoiding hidden magic like dynamic imports)

Reintroducing Friction: The speakers advocate for slowing down. They recommend identifying specific, high-stakes areas (such as database migrations or permission changes) where human judgment is non-negotiable and must be intentionally re-inserted into the development process
Conclusion

Complex Architecture: Discussing scenarios where tools are themselves agents that need LLM access.
Explaining Sampling: Detailing how sampling solves the problem of every agent needing its own LLM by allowing tools to "piggyback" on the client's LLM access.
